newsitem.title: USA: Edison looks to line up new revenue sources.
newsitem.headline: Edison looks to line up new revenue sources.

text.p: In a bid for new sources of revenue, Edison International, parent of Southern California Edison Co, is seeking to deploy its expertise in electricity to a wider range of business applications.
"In the old days we would just focus on our own operations," said Stephen McKenery, project manager for research and technology applications at SoCal Edison.

But industry deregulation has spurred a renewed focus on previously marginal technologies such as solar power and new uses for satellite systems and other products developed by Edison for its own use.
Paul Klein, an Edison spokesman noted, "We are positioning ourselves for 1998."
Under state legislation passed last year, California consumers will be able to choose their electricity supplier starting next January.

The shift is expected to eventually cost traditional monopoly utilities, such as Edison, a significant portion of their customer base, particularly large industrial users, who will be able to negotiate bulk power deals.
Edison expects to continue serving electricity consumers, but will buy most of its power from other producers, then distribute it to residential and small commercial end-users.
The utility plans to auction off later this year all of its thermal generating plants in California, a move which exceeds state regulatory requirements that 50 percent of those assets be divested.
Under California's restructuring legislation, Edison will keep its nuclear and hydroelectric assets, but a decision on its out-of-state, coal-fired assets has not been made.
McKenery said margins on the electric generation side of the business are expected to narrow sharply as "cutthroat" competition between suppliers takes hold.
As a result, Edison aims to continue its role as a regulated distributor of power, but foresees the bulk of future growth in services and related operations.
"All of the Edison affiliates are getting into services. That's where the growth is. We are developing products with national and international appeal," McKenery said.

McKenery said Edison - owner of behemouths such as the 2,200 megawatt San Onofre nuclear plant - hopes to capitalize on a trend toward smaller power generation sources targeted to supply nearby businesses or groups of end-users.
"Solar is a nice piece of that," he noted, citing Edison's recent installation of a 100 kilowatt solar photovoltaic project in a Los Angeles suburb.
The utility is also helping to develop "dual use" products integrating solar technology with building materials.
Although solar power has been around since the 1960s space program, new technology has lowered the costs, McKenery said.
Edison is also looking to market satellite systems which the utility has used to monitor and control distant operations such as substations in the Sierra Mountains.

The utility also hopes to take the lead in marketing of power line and telephone poles made of composite materials to replace wood poles, which have to be injected with pesticides and other toxic materials.
Other projects include working with farmers and business owners to streamline operations and cut electricity bills.

In addition to the utility, Edison International subsidiaries include include Edison Mission Energy, a developer and operator of independent power projects in the U.S. and worldwide, and Edison Capital, which provides financial services to energy firms.

Last year the company launched Edison EV to focus on the development of electric transportation, Edison Source, an unregulated power marketing and retail services division and Edison Select, which will develop consumer products that build on the Edison brand for the mass retail market.

According to Edison's 1996 annual report, earnings from Mission Energy accounted for 12.8 percent of its $717 million total reported earnings last year, up sharply from close to 8.7 percent of its $739 million total 1995 earnings.
Earnings from Edison Capital were 5.7 percent of the total, up from 5.3 percent in 1995, while earnings from the utility accounted for 86.6 percent, down from 86.8 percent.
